doc.q: What is Infantile Refsum Disease?
doc.ref: Infantile Refsum disease (IRD) is a medical condition within the Zellweger spectrum of perixisome biogenesis disorders (PBDs), inherited genetic disorders that damage the white matter of the brain and affect motor movements. PBDs are part of a larger group of disorders called the leukodystrophies. The Zellweger spectrum of PBDs include related, but not more severe, disorders referred to as Zellweger syndrome (ZS) and neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy. Collectively, these disorders are caused by inherited defects in any one of 12 genes, called PEX genes, which are required for the normal formation and function of peroxisomes. Peroxisomes are cell structures required for the normal formation and function of the brain, eyes, liver, kidneys, and bone. They contain enzymes that break down toxic substances in the cells, including very long chain fatty acids and phytanic acid (a type of fat found in certain foods), and synthesize certain fatty materials (lipids) that are required for cell function. When peroxisomes are not functioning, there is over-accumulation of very long chain fatty acids and phytanic acid, and a lack of bile acids and plasmalogens--specialized lipids found in cell membranes and the myelin sheaths and encase and protect nerve fibers.. IRD has some residual perixisome function, resulting in less severe disease than in Zellweger syndrome. Symptoms of IRD begin in infancy with retinitis pigmentosa, a visual impairment that often leads to blindness, and hearing problems that usually progress to deafness by early childhood. Other symptoms may include rapid, jerky eye movements (nystagmus); floppy muscle tone (hypotonia) and lack of muscle coordination (ataxia); mental and growth disabilities; abnormal facial features; enlarged liver; and white matter abnormalities of brain myelin. At the mildest extreme of the disorder, intellect may be preserved. Although Adult Refsum disease and IRD have similar names, they are separate disorders caused by different gene defects.

resps: Infantile refsum disease (IRD) refers to the most severe form of an inherited disorder called refractory cerebellar degeneration, which causes progressive loss of nerve cells and brain tissue that control movement. The signs and symptoms typically appear within 6 months after birth but may vary from child to child; however they usually begin before age two years old. Affected infants have difficulty coordinating movements such as sitting up on their own without support, crawling, standing unassisted, walking while holding onto furniture, etc., although some children can walk independently by about one year of age. They also experience delayed development of speech skills including babbling at around six months of age followed later by limited use of words beginning between ages three and five. Other features include muscle weakness affecting both arms equally when trying to move them together ("adducting" each arm), involuntary jerking motions known as myoclonus involving muscles used during chewing, swallowing, speaking, breathing, eye blinking, facial expressions, head turning side-to-side, neck flexion/extension, trunk rotation, limb extension/flexion, hand grasping/grinding teeth, tongue protrusion/retraction, jaw clenching/clamping down, eyelid fluttering/squinting, lip pursed/thrust forward, mouth opening wide, nose flaring outwards, chin sticking out forwards, shoulder shrugging upwards/downward, hip abduction/adduction, knee buckling inward/outward, ankle dorsiflection/plantarflexion, heel elevation/depression, toe spreading apart/toe curling into foot arches). Some affected individuals develop seizures starting anytime from infancy through adolescence depending upon severity of condition. IRD results from mutations in either PEX7 gene located near end of chromosome Xp21-30 region where it's found only once per cell - this location was previously thought not to be associated with any genetic conditions until recently confirmed via DNA sequencing studies showing several families having been diagnosed based solely off clinical findings rather than molecular testing due to lack availability of specific tests available then. In addition there has now been identified another mutation causing similar presentation described under name "refractoriness syndrome". This new finding suggests that more research needs to be done regarding potential overlap among these disorders since many people who were initially suspected/refracted had actually suffered from other forms instead resulting in misdiagnosis leading researchers believe need further study needed so proper management strategies could be developed accordingly along with better understanding underlying mechanisms involved throughout life span especially considering recent advances made towards developing targeted therapies targeting protein production pathways responsible

doc.q: What causes Juvenile primary lateral sclerosis?
doc.ref: What causes juvenile primary lateral sclerosis? Juvenile primary lateral sclerosis is caused by mutations in the ALS2 gene. The ALS2 gene provides instructions for making a protein called alsin. Alsin is abundant in motor neurons, but its function is not fully understood. Mutations in the ALS2 gene alter the instructions for producing alsin. As a result, alsin is unstable and decays rapidly, or it is disabled and cannot function properly. It is unclear how the loss of functional alsin protein damages motor neurons and causes juvenile primary lateral sclerosis.

resps: Is juvenile PLS inherited? In most cases, the cause of juvenile PLS is unknown (idiopathic). However, it has been reported to be familial and autosomal dominant; this means that one copy of an altered gene from each parent can increase your risk of developing the condition. The genetic change responsible for causing some families' forms of juvenile PLS remains unidentified at present. Researchers have identified several genes associated with adult-onset ALS but not yet found any association between these same genes and juvenile onset disease. It's important to note that while there may be family members who develop similar symptoms as those affected by juvenile PLS, they do so much later than age 40 years old. This difference suggests that different underlying mechanisms might be involved depending on when signs and symptoms first appear during life. As such, people diagnosed with juvenile PLS should discuss their concerns about having children directly with their healthcare provider if possible. A detailed discussion regarding reproductive options will help ensure informed decision-making based upon individual needs rather than assumptions made due solely to parental concern over passing down a potentially fatal disorder which could affect future generations through inheritance patterns described above. More research into how specific mutations within certain genes lead specifically only to early-onset features would greatly improve our understanding of what makes someone more likely to get juvenile PLS compared with other types of motor neuron diseases like spinal muscular atrophy where we know exactly why individuals become symptomatic earlier versus later throughout adulthood. For example: - If you're concerned because both parents had childhood polio then chances go up significantly since many kids born after WWII were infected via contaminated food supplies before vaccines became available until late '50s/early '60s. It is unclear how the loss of functional alsin protein damages motor neurons and causes juvenile primary lateral sclerosis.

Is juvenile PLS inherited? In most cases, the cause of juvenile PLS is unknown (idiopathic). However, it has been reported to be familial and autosomal dominant; this means that one copy of an altered gene from each parent can increase your risk of developing the condition. The genetic change responsible for causing some families' forms of juvenile PLS remains unidentified at present. Researchers have identified several genes associated with adult-onset ALS but not yet found any association between these same genes and juvenile onset disease. It's important to note that while there may be family members who develop similar symptoms as those affected by juvenile PLS, they do so much later than age 40 years old. This difference suggests that different underlying mechanisms might be involved depending on when signs and symptoms first appear during life. As such, people diagnosed with juvenile PLS should discuss their concerns about having children directly with their healthcare provider if possible. A detailed discussion regarding reproductive options will help ensure informed decision-making based upon individual needs rather than assumptions made due solely to parental concern over passing down a potentially fatal disorder which could affect future generations through inheritance patterns described above. doc.q: Is monilethrix inherited?
doc.ref: Monilethrix can have multiple patterns of inheritance. When the condition is caused by a mutation in one of the keratin genes, it is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. In rare cases, the condition results from a new mutation in the gene and is not inherited. When the condition is caused by mutations in the DSG4 gene, it is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, which means both copies of the gene in each cell have mutations. The parents of an individual with an autosomal recessive condition each carry one copy of the mutated gene, but they typically do not show signs and symptoms of the condition.

resps: Monilethrix is usually an autosomal dominant condition, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. In most cases, affected individuals have no history of this feature within their family and acquire it as part of new mutations (de novo). Rarely, people inherit the mutation from another person who has been diagnosed with monilethrix; however, these families do not appear to be at increased risk of having more than one child with the same abnormality because they tend to carry only 1 mutated allele instead of two copies that would lead to reduced production of keratin proteins. A few reports suggest that some forms of monilethrix may follow X-linked inheritance patterns depending on whether there's evidence of genetic linkage between the disease-causing genes involved and sex chromosomes. However, studies indicate that many other conditions can also affect hair shafts such as lichen planopilaris, alopecia totalis/areatae, trichorrhexis nodosa, pili torti, vitiligo, psoriasis vulgaris, seborrheic dermatitis, eczema atopica, scalp ringworm infections caused by Malassezia yeast species, fungal nail infection called tinea unguum, chronic sunburn causing premature aging effects known as photoaging, and even certain types of cancer including basal-cell carcinoma skin tumors affecting eyelashes. These disorders all result in thinning of hairs but don't necessarily involve abnormalities similar to those seen when someone inherits monilethrix. The term "monilethrix" comes from Greek words meaning thread-like ("mono") and twisted threads ("lethe"). This name reflects how the strands look under microscopic examination: very fine, straight fibers arranged side-by-side like beads on string. Under normal circumstances, individual human cells produce several different kinds of protein filaments inside them - microtubules made up mostly of alpha-actin molecules, intermediate filament networks composed mainly of desmosome-associated type I cytokeratins, and cytoskeletal structures formed primarily out of beta-tubulin subunits along with gamma tubuline units. Monilethrix occurs due to defects involving any combination of three major components needed during formation of healthy hair follicles namely matured fibroblasts producing functional keratinocytes through differentiation processes leading eventually towards maturation into specialized epidermal stem cells capable of dividing indefinitely without losing function while maintaining contact points necessary for communication among neighboring cells via gap junction channels connecting adjacent cells together across membranes separating them apart so that

doc.q: What is Hepatitis B?
doc.ref: Your liver is the largest organ inside your body. It helps your body digest food, store energy, and remove poisons. Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver. One type, hepatitis B, is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). Hepatitis B spreads by contact with an infected person's blood, semen, or other body fluid. An infected woman can give hepatitis B to her baby at birth. If you get HBV, you may feel as if you have the flu. You may also have jaundice, a yellowing of skin and eyes, dark-colored urine, and pale bowel movements. Some people have no symptoms at all. A blood test can tell if you have it. HBV usually gets better on its own after a few months. If it does not get better, it is called chronic HBV, which lasts a lifetime. Chronic HBV can lead to scarring of the liver, liver failure, or liver cancer. There is a vaccine for HBV. It requires three shots. All babies should get the vaccine, but older children and adults can get it too. If you travel to countries where Hepatitis B is common, you should get the vaccine. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

doc.q: What are the genetic changes related to Zellweger spectrum disorder?
doc.ref: Mutations in at least 12 genes have been found to cause Zellweger spectrum disorder. These genes provide instructions for making a group of proteins known as peroxins, which are essential for the formation and normal functioning of cell structures called peroxisomes. Peroxisomes are sac-like compartments that contain enzymes needed to break down many different substances, including fatty acids and certain toxic compounds. They are also important for the production of fats (lipids) used in digestion and in the nervous system. Peroxins assist in the formation (biogenesis) of peroxisomes by producing the membrane that separates the peroxisome from the rest of the cell and by importing enzymes into the peroxisome. Mutations in the genes that cause Zellweger spectrum disorder prevent peroxisomes from forming normally. Diseases that disrupt the formation of peroxisomes, including Zellweger spectrum disorder, are called peroxisome biogenesis disorders. If the production of peroxisomes is altered, these structures cannot perform their usual functions. The signs and symptoms of Zellweger syndrome are due to the absence of functional peroxisomes within cells. NALD and infantile Refsum disease are caused by mutations that allow some peroxisomes to form. Mutations in the PEX1 gene are the most common cause of Zellweger spectrum disorder and are found in nearly 70 percent of affected individuals. The other genes associated with Zellweger spectrum disorder each account for a smaller percentage of cases of this condition.

These benign tumor formations may cause no symptoms unless their location interferes with normal functioning of nearby organs or tissues. In some cases, however, malignant transformation of the fibroblasts within the tumor cells leads to cancerous lesions called schwannomas which grow slowly over time without causing noticeable signs or symptoms until later stages when they become large enough to press against surrounding structures thereby interfering with organ functions. doc.q: What is bradyopsia?
doc.ref: Bradyopsia is a rare condition that affects vision. The term "bradyopsia" is from the Greek words for slow vision. In affected individuals, the eyes adapt more slowly than usual to changing light conditions. For example, people with this condition are blinded for several seconds when going from a dark environment into a bright one, such as when walking out of a darkened movie theater into daylight. Their eyes also have trouble adapting from bright light to dark conditions, such as when driving into a dark tunnel on a sunny day. Some people with bradyopsia also have difficulty seeing some moving objects, particularly small objects moving against a bright background. As a result, they often have trouble watching or participating in sports with a ball, such as soccer or tennis. People with bradyopsia can have reduced sharpness (acuity) of vision, although acuity may depend on the conditions under which vision is tested. Visual acuity may appear to be severely affected if it is tested under bright lights, but it can be near normal if tested in a dim environment. The ability to see colors and distinguish between them is normal. The vision problems associated with bradyopsia become apparent in early childhood. They are usually stable, which means they do not worsen over time.

doc.q: What are the genetic changes related to spondylothoracic dysostosis?
doc.ref: The MESP2 gene provides instructions for a protein that plays a critical role in the development of vertebrae. Specifically, it is involved in separating vertebrae from one another during early development, a process called somite segmentation. Mutations in the MESP2 gene prevent the production of any protein or lead to the production of an abnormally short, nonfunctional protein. When the MESP2 protein is nonfunctional or absent, somite segmentation does not occur properly, which results in the malformation and fusion of the bones of the spine and ribs seen in spondylothoracic dysostosis.

resps: Mutations in at least three genes have been found to cause S-TDO: COL2A1, FBN1 and TGFBR3 (also known as ACVRL). These mutations account for most cases of this condition; however, researchers continue to search for other gene defects that may be responsible for some affected individuals who do not carry any identified mutation. The proteins produced from these genes play important roles during development before birth when bones form properly throughout life. Mutations in each of these genes lead to an abnormal protein whose function is unknown but likely disrupts normal bone formation early on in embryonic development. As a result, many parts of the skeleton develop abnormally after conception begins. Researchers believe that abnormalities involving collagen type II, which results from mutations in the COL2A1 gene, underlie much of what happens in people with S-TDO because they can also affect cartilage growth prior to birth. Collagen types I and III make up about 90 percent of all body tissue except skin cells where it makes up more than half of their structure. They provide strength and flexibility to connective tissues such as tendons, ligaments, blood vessels, muscles, joints, and organs like the heart valves and lungs' air sacs called alveoli. In addition, collagens help maintain the shape of bones by providing them with tensile strength so they don't break easily while allowing enough elasticity to absorb shocks caused by movement. However, only one-third of the total amount of collagen type II exists within our bodies inside the matrix surrounding developing long-bone ends between childhood infancy and adolescence. This particular location allows scientists to study how mutations affecting collagen type II might influence skeletal development later in life. It has become clear now that there's no single "cause" behind the various features associated with S-TDO. Instead, multiple factors appear to interact together over time to produce different signs and symptoms seen among those diagnosed with this disorder. For example, studies suggest that certain combinations of mutations in specific regions of either the COL2A1 or FBN1 gene could increase susceptibility to having short stature without causing severe joint problems characteristic of S-TDO. Other research indicates that variations in several non-coding DNA sequences near both copies of the TGFBR3 gene contribute significantly toward determining whether someone will experience mild forms versus moderate-to-severe versions of this disease state depending upon inherited patterns from parents carrying similar variants themselves. doc.q: How many people are affected by X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata 2?
doc.ref: X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata 2 has been estimated to affect fewer than 1 in 400,000 newborns. However, the disorder may actually be more common than this estimate because it is likely underdiagnosed, particularly in females with mild signs and symptoms. More than 95 percent of cases of X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata 2 occur in females. About a dozen males with the condition have been reported in the scientific literature.

resps: X-CDP2 is estimated to affect between one and two per million newborns worldwide, although the condition may be underdiagnosed because it can have mild signs that go unnoticed until later childhood. The prevalence of this disorder has been reported as approximately three times higher among individuals from Japan than those living elsewhere; however, studies suggest that these findings were based on an incomplete understanding of how CDPS1 mutations cause CDP type II symptoms (i.e., whether they result only from loss-of-function changes). More recent research suggests that all cases of xeroderma pigmentosum-like syndrome caused by CDPS1 gene defects actually represent different forms of cataract-related syndromes rather than distinct disorders such as X-CDP2. As a consequence, some researchers believe that there should no longer be separate diagnostic categories for each form of cataract-associated syndrome but instead recognize them together as part of what was previously called "xeroderma pigmentosum-like" syndrome. It remains unclear if Japanese children who develop early-onset severe eye problems will eventually also experience other features associated with X-CDP2 including hearing impairment, intellectual disability, short stature, skeletal abnormalities, delayed development, seizures, and/or behavioral issues. In addition, more detailed genetic testing could help clarify which specific mutation causes particular clinical characteristics so that targeted therapies might become available someday soon. However, at present most patients do not receive any therapy beyond supportive care aimed at treating their individual needs.

doc.q: What are the symptoms of Gastrointestinal Carcinoid Tumors?
doc.ref: Some gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors have no signs or symptoms in the early stages.Signs and symptoms may be caused by the growth of the tumor and/or the hormones the tumor makes. Some tumors, especially tumors of the stomach or appendix, may not cause signs or symptoms. Carcinoid tumors are often found during tests or treatments for other conditions. Carcinoid tumors in the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, and ileum), colon, and rectum sometimes cause signs or symptoms as they grow or because of the hormones they make. Other conditions may cause the same signs or symptoms. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Duodenum Signs and symptoms of GI carcinoid tumors in the duodenum (first part of the small intestine, that connects to the stomach) may include the following: - Abdominal pain. - Constipation. - Diarrhea. - Change in stool color. - Nausea. - Vomiting. - Jaundice (yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes). - Heartburn. - Jejunum and ileum Signs and symptoms of GI carcinoid tumors in the jejunum (middle part of the small intestine) and ileum (last part of the small intestine, that connects to the colon) may include the following: - Abdominal pain. - Weight loss for no known reason. - Feeling very tired. - Feeling bloated - Diarrhea. - Nausea. - Vomiting. - Colon Signs and symptoms of GI carcinoid tumors in the colon may include the following: - Abdominal pain. - Weight loss for no known reason. - Rectum Signs and symptoms of GI carcinoid tumors in the rectum may include the following: - Blood in the stool. - Pain in the rectum. - Constipation.

doc.q: What are the genetic changes related to 15q13.3 microdeletion?
doc.ref: Most people with a 15q13.3 microdeletion are missing a sequence of about 2 million DNA building blocks (base pairs), also written as 2 megabases (Mb), at position q13.3 on chromosome 15. The exact size of the deleted region varies, but it typically contains at least six genes. This deletion usually affects one of the two copies of chromosome 15 in each cell. The signs and symptoms that can result from a 15q13.3 microdeletion are probably related to the loss of one or more genes in this region. However, it is unclear which missing genes contribute to the specific features of the disorder. Because some people with a 15q13.3 microdeletion have no obvious signs or symptoms, researchers believe that other genetic or environmental factors may also be involved.

resps: The deletion of DNA at chromosome band q13.3 on one copy (the maternal) of each cell is associated with this condition, although it can also occur when inherited from either parent and may be present only in some cells due to an error called mosaicism during early embryonic development. The region that has been deleted contains several genes whose functions have not yet been determined; however researchers believe these gene deletions likely contribute to intellectual disability by disrupting normal brain function before birth. In addition, people who carry two copies of the chromosomal change instead of just one tend to experience more severe symptoms than those carrying only one copy. Researchers suspect other factors such as environmental influences play roles in determining how much damage occurs after the initial loss of genetic material. Some individuals do not appear to have any signs or symptoms caused by their specific chromosomal abnormality but still show features consistent with IDDM syndrome because they lack certain proteins produced by the missing genes. These cases suggest additional mutations outside the affected area might cause similar problems. It remains unclear why many children born into families without known history of IDDM syndrome develop learning disabilities while others don't. However, studies indicate that there appears to be no relationship between having siblings with developmental delay/IDDM syndrome and developing delayed speech skills themselves. This suggests that different mechanisms underlie individual differences among family members regarding whether they will exhibit characteristic behaviors linked to IDDM syndrome. Other conditions involving multiple areas of dysfunction including autism spectrum disorders share similarities with IDDM syndrome so both could result from overlapping causes rather than separate ones. For example, research indicates that about half of all autistic boys inherit a mutation affecting another part of the genome which disrupts communication within nerve cells leading them to malfunction properly resulting in behavioral issues seen in ASD's like social withdrawal etc.. A few recent reports describe girls diagnosed with IDDM syndrome showing characteristics typical of Rett Syndrome -a disorder characterized primarily by impaired movement coordination along side cognitive difficulties-which further supports evidence suggesting shared underlying biological processes causing various forms of neurodevelopmental impairment across populations worldwide today! It remains unclear why many children born into families without known history of IDDM syndrome develop learning disabilities while others don't. However, studies indicate that there appears to be no relationship between having siblings with developmental delay/IDDM syndrome and developing delayed speech skills themselves. This suggests that different mechanisms underlie individual differences among family members regarding whether they will exhibit characteristic behaviors linked to IDDM syndrome. Other conditions involving multiple areas of dysfunction including autism spectrum disorders share similarities with IDDM syndrome so both could result from overlapping causes rather than separate ones. For example, research indicates that about half of all autistic boys inherit a mutation affecting another part of the genome which disrupts communication within nerve cells leading them to malfunction properly resulting in behavioral issues seen in ASD's like social withdrawal etc.. A few recent reports describe girls diagnosed with IDDM syndrome showing characteristics typical of Rett Syndrome -a disorder characterized primarily by impaired movement coordination along side cognitive difficulties-which further supports evidence suggesting shared underlying biological processes causing various forms of neurodevelopmental impairment across populations worldwide today! doc.q: How to diagnose Kidney Stones in Children?
doc.ref: The process of diagnosing any illness begins with consideration of the symptoms. Pain or bloody urine may be the first symptom. Urine, blood, and imaging tests will help determine whether symptoms are caused by a stone. Urine tests can be used to check for infection and for substances that form stones. Blood tests can be used to check for biochemical problems that can lead to kidney stones. Various imaging techniques can be used to locate the stone: - Ultrasound uses a device, called a transducer, that bounces safe, painless sound waves off organs to create an image of their structure. An abdominal ultrasound can create images of the entire urinary tract. The procedure is performed in a health care providers office, outpatient center, or hospital by a specially trained technician, and the images are interpreted by a radiologista doctor who specializes in medical imaging; anesthesia is not needed. The images can show the location of any stones. This test does not expose children to radiation, unlike some other imaging tests. Although other tests are more useful in detecting very small stones or stones in the lower portion of the ureter, ultrasound is considered by many health care providers to be the best screening test to look for stones. - Computerized tomography (CT) scans use a combination of x rays and computer technology to create threedimensional (3-D) images. A CT scan may include the injection of a special dye, called contrast medium. CT scans require the child to lie on a table that slides into a tunnel-shaped device where the x rays are taken. The procedure is performed in an outpatient center or hospital by an x-ray technician, and the images are interpreted by a radiologist; anesthesia is not needed. CT scans may be required to get an accurate stone count when children are being considered for urologic surgery. Because CT scans expose children to a moderate amount of radiation, health care providers try to reduce radiation exposure in children by avoiding repeated CT scans, restricting the area scanned as much as possible, and using the lowest radiation dose that will provide the needed diagnostic information. - X-ray machines use radiation to create images of the childs urinary tract. The images can be taken at an outpatient center or hospital by an x-ray technician, and the images are interpreted by a radiologist; anesthesia is not needed. The x rays are used to locate many kinds of stones. A conventional x ray is generally less informative than an ultrasound or CT scan, but it is less expensive and can be done more quickly than other imaging procedures.

resps: A health care provider will use the following tests and procedures to help make an accurate diagnosis of kidney stones: - Physical exam, including checking blood pressure levels -- high blood pressure can be caused by chronic renal failure (kidneys that do not work well). A physical examination is done during which a doctor uses touch to feel organs such as the kidneys; check pulses at certain points on each arm and leg; listen to sounds made when air moves through lungs and arteries using a stethoscope; and look into eyes for signs of damage from glomerulonephritis. The child's height may also be measured because short stature often occurs if there has been long-term loss of protein due to kidney disease. In addition, urine samples collected over 24 hours might be tested to see how much creatinine remains after urination. Creatinine level reflects muscle mass but does not reflect total body size accurately. This test helps determine whether growth hormone deficiency exists. For more detailed information about these diagnostic methods, go to "Kidney Stone Diagnosis." If no other cause seems likely, imaging studies should be used to confirm presence of stone(s) within one or both kidneys before beginning any therapy. Imaging techniques include ultrasonography, computed tomography scan (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), intravenous pyelogram (IVP), excretory urography, radionuclide scanning, x-ray films, and voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG). Ultrasonic B-Scan ultrasound provides images created by sound waves bouncing off internal structures called echoes. An experienced technician performs this procedure while placing gel between your skin and transducer device placed just under the surface of the abdomen where it bounces against tissues inside the body. These echo signals create pictures showing anatomy and movement of soft tissue like muscles and organs. Ultrasound exams require little preparation except wearing comfortable clothing without metal fasteners. CT scans involve injecting special dye directly into a vein so you'll have better contrast than regular X-rays show. You lie still on a table that slides past an opening in a large machine shaped like a donut. As part of the process, you're given mild sedation along with pain medicine to keep you relaxed throughout the study. Afterward, you return home immediately unless instructed otherwise. MRI machines produce very strong magnets combined with radio waves to take pictures of areas deep inside the body. During the procedure, you remain lying down on a narrow bed that passes through the center of the magnet. To reduce noise produced by the scanner, earplugs or headphones are

resps: Freeman-Sherlock syndrome is estimated to affect 1 per million individuals worldwide, although the condition may be underdiagnosed because its signs and symptoms can vary widely among affected families. The prevalence of this disorder has been reported as approximately one case every two thousand births; however, it appears that some cases have not yet been identified due to their mild features being mistaken for other conditions such as myotonia congenita (a muscle disease). In addition, there appear to be more females than males who develop this condition at birth but do not show any associated health problems later on during childhood. This gender difference suggests an X-linked inheritance pattern rather than autosomal recessive transmission since only boys would inherit both copies of the mutated gene from each parent if they were male carriers while girls could also pass down either copy depending upon which was inherited through her father's side alone when she had no sons herself - making them less likely overall compared against all others including those without children themselves! However recent studies suggest otherwise suggesting instead that most women actually carry just one defective version whereas men usually get two so causing much greater severity especially early-onset forms like infantile onset type A where babies don't survive past infancy unless treated aggressively enough before age three years old...which makes sense why we see fewer reports about these types now given advances made over time regarding better treatments available today allowing survival beyond five year mark even though still quite rare occurrence globally across populations throughout history up until recently anyway thanks largely too our improved understanding & management strategies applied specifically towards treating infants born prematurely etc whom doctors previously couldn’t treat effectively back then leading directly toward increased life expectancy rates observed currently amongst survivors diagnosed after ages six months onwards into adulthood
